prize_parts.citation: For incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, and thereby explaining exporter selection, reallocation across firms and new channels for the gains from trade.

statement.case_for: Moving from industry-level to firm-level analysis changed how trade is modelled, measured and evaluated. The framework explains why only some firms export, why trade reallocates resources toward more productive firms, and why this creates a gains-from-trade channel beyond comparative advantage and scale economies. It connects to micro data, to growth and productivity, and to the reallocation questions macroeconomists care about. It has also generated a large quantitative literature, and over two decades of testing have established it. The attribution is the cleanest on my list: Melitz (2003) is the core model, and Helpman's broader theoretical programme, including the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work on exporting versus FDI, completes it. In my opening I ranked the New Keynesian ballot (B037) first, and I still value its policy influence. But the opening statements show that the credit there is not settled. Colleagues propose different triads (Calvo, Gali or Christiano-Eichenbaum, alongside Taylor and Woodford), and any three-name cut leaves out major contributors. I therefore move B010 to the top, because the scientific contribution is large and the credit assignment is more defensible.
statement.case_against: Trade was recognised in 2008 for new trade theory, so the Committee may weigh field balance. The credit for firm heterogeneity is also not fully captured by the two names. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and Hopenhayn in the firm-dynamics literature, are important precursors or parallel contributors who are not credited. Redding is omitted from my pair. The quantitative size of the selection gains also depends on parametric assumptions, such as Pareto productivity draws. I am relying on my own knowledge of the literature and have not independently verified the record.

responses.point: Boppart ranked B010 sixth and asked whether it is a distinct advance beyond Krugman's 2008 recognition of new trade theory.
responses.response: I think it is distinct. Krugman's work concerns increasing returns and monopolistic competition at the level of the industry, with symmetric firms. Melitz and Helpman add within-industry heterogeneity and selection. This produces different empirical implications on exporter premia, firm entry and exit, and reallocation as a source of welfare gains, and these have been tested on firm-level data. That is a new discovery rather than a refinement. I accept that the Committee should word the citation so that it does not overlap with the 2008 citation, and I have framed mine around selection and reallocation.

responses.point: Hassler ranked B010 first but flagged that the Committee may want Eaton-Kortum or Bernard-Jensen pioneers credited, and that Helpman may be seen in a broader lifetime-achievement framing.
responses.response: I take the precursor concern seriously, but I do not think it undermines the core pair. The Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum line is a parallel Ricardian and empirical strand, while the heterogeneous-firm selection mechanism and its extension to FDI are credited clearly to Melitz and to Helpman with his co-authors. The citation should therefore be narrow, focused on selection and reallocation, not on trade theory in general. A lifetime-achievement framing for Helpman would weaken the case because it would obscure what is being rewarded. I would keep the citation tied to the specific discovery, and I would not adopt a laureate set that tries to cover every precursor.

responses.point: Friberg ranked B037 first, arguing that the New Keynesian framework and policy-rule analysis underpin modern central-bank practice and that the timing is ripe.
responses.response: I agree on influence and ranked B037 first myself. The disagreement is about attribution. Friberg's triad (Woodford, Taylor, Gali) differs from mine (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford), and the other openings propose still other combinations. Whether the Committee can defend any of them is the main open question, and I would not settle it by a vote count. The post-2021 inflation episode also makes the framework's empirical record more contested than the case for B010. I keep B037 as an alternative, and I would support it if the Committee finds a defensible boundary for the credit.

responses.point: Strömberg ranked B019 first and argues that the Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism and the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist financial accelerator together form the credit-friction paradigm, which would justify including Gertler.
responses.response: I agree that B019 is an important foundational contribution, and I ranked it third. But I would keep the credit to the originators of the collateral-constraint mechanism, Kiyotaki and Moore. The accelerator strand overlaps with Bernanke's recognition in 2022, and adding Gertler brings in the same attribution difficulty that troubles B037, since Gertler also appears on that ballot. Direct empirical identification of the amplification channel is also less settled than the theory's influence suggests. I regard B019 as a strong alternative, not as the first choice.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats heterogeneous-firm trade as sufficiently separate from the 2008 recognition of new trade theory.
Whether credit for Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, or for Redding, should alter the laureate set or the wording of the citation.
Whether B037 can be given a defensible three-name boundary, and how the post-2021 inflation episode should weigh in the assessment.
How much weight the Committee gives to field balance after the 2022 financial-crisis prize and the 2024 institutions prize when comparing B019 and B010.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to the credited names on B010, B037 or B019 is apparent from my supplied profile. I have co-authored with Timo Boppart (co-opted member) and have long-term co-authors including John Hassler (chair). Neither is a credited candidate on my proposed ballot. Torsten Persson, credited on B039, is a past Committee member, which I note for disclosure only. I ranked B039 sixth.
